voice: Wholesale-led but readable to homeowners. No call to action - the caption ends on the substance. Specs are stated plainly, never dressed up. Claims are limited to what DK already publishes on its own artwork: up to 85% energy saving, 50,000+ hours, 2-year warranty, 180-265V wide voltage, flicker-free operation, 3000K/4000K/6500K options.
notes: First line is the hook - it is the only text visible before 'more', so it carries the keywords.
Hashtag sets are deliberately varied post to post. An identical block on every upload reads as automation.
No city hashtags are used anywhere. DK's location was never confirmed, and a wrong city pulls the wrong leads. Add them once the city is known.
Products with multiple images (six 15W panels, four 20W, four 24W) each get a different angle - spec, install, energy, trade, room, comparison - so the repeats do not read as repeats.
The 'group' field drives schedule interleaving: same-group posts are never scheduled on adjacent days.
No call to action: DK's captions end on the information itself. Nothing asks the reader to message, DM or click.

posts.caption:
120 LEDs per metre, and 100 metres on a single roll.

One roll covers a full floor of cove lighting without a join. That matters more than it sounds - every splice in a strip run is a future failure point and a visible bright spot on the ceiling.

6.8mm wide, so it drops into a standard aluminium channel. Wide voltage 180-265V, which is the specification that keeps a strip alive on Pakistani mains.

Wholesale rates on full rolls.

88 LEDs per metre is where the dotting stops.

Run a low-density strip behind a diffuser and you can count the individual points of light through it. At 88/m the beam merges into one line before it reaches the cover - which is the entire reason to spec density rather than just wattage.

70m roll, 6.8mm profile, 180-265V input range.

Sample lengths available for dealers.

288 LEDs a metre. No dots, no hotspots, just one continuous line.

COB neon is the answer when the light source itself is on show - signage, stair noses, under-counter, profile letters. Because the diodes sit under a single phosphor layer instead of behind a lens, you get an unbroken glow you can bend around a curve without seeing the seam.

8mm profile, 10W per metre, 100m roll.

15W adjustable panel - the one that fixes a ceiling you cannot move.

The bezel tilts, so the light lands where the room needs it rather than straight down onto the floor. Useful when the ceiling grid was set before anyone decided where the sofa or the artwork was going.

Flicker-free driver, 180-265V, 50,000+ hours rated life, 2-year warranty.

Available in 3000K, 4000K and 6500K.

180-265V. That range is the whole reason this panel outlives the cheap ones.

Mains here does not sit politely at 220V. It sags at peak load and spikes when the load drops off. A driver built for a narrow window cooks itself over a few months of that - which is why so many panels fail long before the LEDs do.

This one is specified across the full 180-265V band and tested against it.

15W, 2-year warranty.

Where a 15W adjustable actually belongs.

Bedrooms, corridors and small retail bays - anywhere the ceiling is under about 9 feet and you want the light aimed at a wall, a wardrobe or a display rather than straight down.

Go 3000K for bedrooms and living rooms, 4000K if it is a working corridor or a shop floor.

15W, flicker-free, 50,000+ hours.

For the dealers asking which panel moves fastest - it is this one.

15W adjustable sits at the price point where a homeowner will buy six without thinking about it, and it solves a problem the fixed panels cannot, so it does not get returned.

Stocked in all three colour temperatures. Consistent batch-to-batch colour, which matters when a customer comes back for two more six months later.

Six of these replace six 60W bulbs and pull less than one of them did.

15W each, so six comes to 90W total. The incandescent set-up they replace was 360W. That gap runs every evening for the life of the fitting, and at 50,000+ rated hours the fitting has a long life to run it over.

Up to 85% energy saving is not a slogan - it is the arithmetic.

Spring clips, one cutout, done in under two minutes.

No separate driver box to find a home for above the ceiling, no fiddling with the tilt after it is seated - set the angle once the bezel is in and it stays where you put it.

Worth checking your cutout before ordering in quantity - the fitting is fixed, the hole is not.

20W adjustable - the step up when 15W leaves the corners dark.

Same tilting bezel, more output. This is the one for living rooms, larger bedrooms and shop floors where the ceiling is a little higher and the throw has further to travel before it does any work.

180-265V, flicker-free, 2-year warranty, 50,000+ hours.

3000K, 4000K or 6500K.

Same 20W panel. Three completely different rooms.

3000K warm white and it reads as a living room. 4000K natural white and the same fitting turns a kitchen into somewhere you can actually prep food. 6500K cool white and it becomes a study or a bathroom.

The wattage sets how much light. The colour temperature sets what the room feels like. Get the second one wrong and no amount of the first one fixes it.

20W adjustable, specified across a retail floor.

Tilt matters more in a shop than anywhere else. Product sits on walls and shelves, not on the floor, so a fixed downlight puts most of its output where nobody is looking. Angle the beam onto the merchandise and the same wattage does twice the work.

Consistent colour across the batch, so a run of twenty reads as one installation rather than twenty separate purchases.

Two-year warranty, and we would rather you never use it.

Most LED panels do not fail at the diode. They fail at the driver - too much heat in too small a housing, running on mains that swings 80 volts either side of nominal. So that is where the cost goes in this one: a driver rated for the full 180-265V range that stays cool enough to see out the LEDs.

50,000+ hours rated. 20W.

24W - the largest adjustable panel in the range.

For high ceilings, double-height spaces and commercial floors where the fitting is a long way from the surface it is meant to light. Everything below this wattage starts to spread thin past about eleven feet.

Tilting bezel, flicker-free driver, 180-265V, 2-year warranty.

All three colour temperatures in stock.

Do not buy this because it says 24W. Buy it for what 24W delivers.

Wattage tells you what a light consumes, not what it produces. Two 24W panels from different factories can differ by a third in actual output, and the number on the box will not tell you which is which.

Ask for lumens. Ask for lm/W. We publish both, because we measure both before anything ships.

24W at 4000K is the office specification.

Warm white makes a workspace feel like a lounge and people stop concentrating. Cool white at 6500K is fine for a lab and punishing for eight hours at a desk. 4000K natural white sits between the two, which is why almost every office that gets it right lands there.

Flicker-free matters doubly here - screen work plus a flickering source is where the headaches come from.

Forty of these on one floor, and every one of them the same white.

Colour consistency across a batch is the thing nobody checks until it is installed and one panel in the row is visibly pinker than the rest. On a large order that is not a cosmetic problem, it is a re-visit.

We bin for colour before packing. On project quantities we will hold stock from the same run.

10W bubble light - small fitting, soft spread.

The domed diffuser is doing the work here. It takes a compact source and opens the beam out wide, so you get a gentle wash instead of a hard circle on the floor directly beneath.

Good for low ceilings, corridors and anywhere a sharp-edged downlight would feel harsh.

180-265V, 50,000+ hours.

The 10W bubble, in the ceiling it was built for.

This is what the wide diffusion actually buys you - no scallops on the wall, no bright pool under each fitting, just an even level across the whole corridor. Spacing gets more forgiving too, which usually means fewer fittings for the same result.

10W each. Warm, natural or cool white.

13W bubble. Same diffuser, three more watts of headroom.

The step from 10W matters most in rooms over about 140 square feet, or where the ceiling is above nine feet. Below that the 10W is the better buy and you are paying for output you will not see.

We would rather tell you that than sell you the bigger one.

180-265V, 2-year warranty.

13W bubble lights, run across a living room ceiling.

The reason these suit a home better than a hard-edged spot: no glare when you are lying on a sofa looking up. A bare COB in the same position is uncomfortable to sit under. The dome spreads the source over a wider area, so the brightness per square centimetre drops and your eye stops noticing it.

3000K for this kind of room.

3W. The smallest thing in the range, and the one that changes a room most.

Accent lighting is not about adding brightness, it is about adding contrast. A 3W COB on a painting, a niche or a stone wall gives the eye somewhere to land. Fill the ceiling with even light and everything flattens out.

Tight beam, clean cut-off, no spill onto the surrounding wall.

Why COB, and not a cluster of small diodes?

Chip-on-board packs the emitters onto a single substrate under one phosphor layer. You get one light source instead of nine, which means one shadow instead of nine overlapping ones. On anything with an edge - a sculpture, a plant, a textured wall - that difference is immediately visible.

5W, tight beam, flicker-free driver.

8W COB is the jewellery-counter wattage.

Enough punch to make metal and stone come alive under glass, tight enough that the beam stays on the product instead of washing across the aisle. Retail lighting lives or dies on that second part.

If you are lighting a display case, beam angle changes the result more than wattage does. Narrow keeps the light on the product; wide spills it across the aisle.

13W COB - for when the ceiling is a long way up.

Beam intensity falls off with the square of the distance. Double the height and you get a quarter of the light on the surface, which is why a 5W that looks perfect at eight feet disappears at sixteen.

This is the one for double-height lobbies, stairwells and showrooms.

180-265V, 50,000+ hours, 2-year warranty.

Stocking question we get a lot: which COB wattage sells?

5W and 13W, and it is not close. 5W is the accent light everyone buys in fours and sixes. 13W is the one contractors specify for anything commercial. The middle sizes move slowly by comparison.

If you are opening an account, start with those two and add from there.

Deluxe 5W - same output, better housing.

The upgrade here is the trim and the heat path. A deeper anti-glare recess so you cannot see the diode from a standing position, and more aluminium behind it to pull heat off the chip. Cooler chip, slower lumen depreciation, longer before the colour starts drifting.

Where the fitting is visible and the budget allows, this is the one.

Anti-glare depth is the spec nobody asks about and everybody notices.

If you can see the bright chip from where you normally stand or sit, the fitting is too shallow. Your pupil closes against that point source and the rest of the room reads darker than it is - so people turn on more lights and wonder why it still feels dim.

Recessed deep enough to cut the source out of normal sightlines.

5W Deluxe.

5W moveable COB. Point it, then re-point it next year.

The gimbal lets the beam swing well off vertical while the trim stays flush to the ceiling. That is the whole idea - you get directional light without a visible fitting hanging below the plasterboard line.

Useful in any room where the furniture is going to move eventually. Which is every room.

7.5W moveable, set about 30 degrees off vertical. That is the art-wall angle.

Steeper than that and the beam skims the surface, picking out every imperfection in the plaster. Shallower and you get a reflection of the source straight back into the viewer's eye off any glazed frame.

Thirty degrees is the number galleries settled on a long time ago. It still works.

Mount adjustable spots away from the wall, not against it.

Common mistake: fittings go in 6 inches from the wall, then get tilted hard over to reach the artwork. The beam arrives at a grazing angle and every bump in the paint throws a shadow.

Set them out about a third of the ceiling height from the wall and the geometry does the work for you.

7.5W moveable COB.

The Sunflower trim, and the reason it is shaped like that.

Those fins are not decoration - they are surface area. More aluminium exposed to the air above the ceiling means the chip runs cooler, and a cooler chip holds its colour and its output for longer.

Heat is what actually kills an LED. Everything else is secondary.

5W COB, 50,000+ hours rated.

7W AK downlight - 112mm cutout.

Write that number down before you order. Cutout is the one dimension that cannot be fixed on site: too small and you are filing plasterboard on a ladder, too large and the trim does not cover the hole.

If you are replacing existing fittings, measure the hole before anything else. 112mm is a common size, and matching it means no patching and no repaint.

The Alpha 7W. Nothing clever about it, which is rather the point.

This is the fitting that goes in by the dozen - corridors, bedrooms, utility spaces, anywhere the lighting just has to work and nobody will ever comment on it. Low wattage, wide enough beam to space out sensibly, flicker-free driver, 180-265V.

The unglamorous half of a lighting schedule is usually the larger half.

Alpha 7W in the 105mm cutout - the retrofit size.

105mm is what a great many older halogen and CFL downlights were cut to. If that is what is coming out of your ceiling, this goes back in with no patching, no filler and no repaint.

Swap a 50W halogen for this and you drop 43W per fitting while getting more light on the floor.

13W at a 120mm cutout - and a spacing rule worth keeping.

Rough guide for even coverage: space downlights at about half your ceiling height. Nine-foot ceiling, fittings roughly four and a half feet apart. Closer and you are wasting fittings, further and you get scallops of light and dark between them.

It is a starting point, not gospel - but it beats guessing.

13W HR - high output in a standard downlight housing.

The usual reason to reach for this one: the ceiling grid is already set, you cannot add more fittings, and the room is coming out darker than the drawing promised. More output per hole solves it without touching the plasterboard.

Flicker-free, 180-265V, 2-year warranty.

Aluminium body, and you can feel the difference before you switch it on.

Plastic-bodied downlights hold heat against the driver. Aluminium moves it out. Over a few thousand hours that is the difference between a fitting that holds its brightness and one that quietly dims and shifts colour while nobody notices.

Weight is a reasonable proxy for build quality here. Pick one up.

13W.

PL-Alum 13W, 120mm cutout. The specification, plainly.

13W draw. Aluminium body. 180-265V input. Flicker-free driver. 50,000+ hours rated life. 2-year warranty. Available 3000K, 4000K, 6500K.

No adjectives. If you are comparing quotes, these are the lines that should be on both of them - and if the other one is missing the voltage range, ask why.

13W here replaces a 100W incandescent downlight. Same light on the floor.

That is 87 watts saved per fitting, every hour it runs. Across twenty fittings in a shop that runs twelve hours a day, the arithmetic gets serious quickly.

The fitting costs more than the bulb it replaces. It stops costing more somewhere in the first year.

Every fin on that housing is there to move heat.

The fluted trim is not styling. It is surface area, sized so the chip behind it runs cool enough to hold its output and its colour for the full 50,000+ hours on the label. A rated life only means something if the thermal design supports it.

Deep anti-glare recess, flush trim, adjustable head.

One roll. Enough to run a full cove without a single join.

Every splice in a strip installation is two things you do not want: a resistance point that runs hot, and a visible break in the line once the diffuser goes on. Buying the length you need on one reel avoids both.

Pre-wired with a mains plug. 180-265V.

Battens. The least glamorous fitting we make, and the one that never comes back.

Kitchens, garages, corridors, workshops, back-of-house in every shop in the country. Surface mounted, so no cutout and no ceiling void needed - which is why they go into buildings that were never designed for recessed lighting.

Linkable end to end for a continuous run.

posts.product: Product range hero - strip, downlight, battens
posts.caption:
Three fittings, one supplier, one warranty to chase.

Strip for the cove, COB downlight for the accents, battens for the utility spaces. Most rooms need all three, and buying them from three different places is how you end up with three different whites on the same ceiling.

Up to 85% energy saving. 50,000+ hours. 2-year warranty. 180-265V across the range.

Wattage is not brightness. It never was.

Watts tell you what a light consumes. Lumens tell you what it produces. The ratio between them - lumens per watt - is the only number that tells you whether a fitting is actually efficient or just underpowered.

A modern 9W LED puts out around 810lm. The 60W incandescent it replaces managed 700-800lm. Same light, a fraction of the power.

Save this one for the next time someone quotes you a wattage and calls it brightness.

3000K, 4000K or 6500K - a room-by-room map.

3000K warm white: bedrooms and living rooms. It reads as relaxed, and it flatters skin and wood.

4000K natural white: kitchens and offices. Neutral enough to see properly by, without the clinical edge.

6500K cool white: study rooms and bathrooms. Crisp, high contrast, keeps you alert.

Get this wrong and no amount of extra wattage will fix how the room feels. Every DK fitting comes in all three.

posts.product: Infographic - contractors cut costs with wholesale LED (portrait)
posts.caption:
How contractors cut lighting costs without cutting quality.

Wholesale pricing on volume. White-label options if you supply under your own name. And project planning support before the order - which is where most of the money is actually saved, because the wrong spec costs more than the wrong price.

What you get either way: drivers rated across the full 180-265V range, flicker-free performance, colour consistency batch to batch, and stock that is actually there when the site needs it.

We test against Pakistani conditions, not laboratory ones.

That means measuring true luminous output rather than trusting the chip datasheet, checking colour consistency across a production batch, and verifying that drivers stay cool and flicker-free across the full 180-265V input range that our mains actually delivers.

A fitting that performs beautifully at a steady 220V and dies at 190V has not really been tested.

Planning a larger project? We will help spec wattages and colour temperatures room by room, and price it once quantities are clear.

The one lighting decision people regret most: colour temperature.

Wattage is easy to change - swap the fitting. Colour temperature gets chosen once, across a whole floor, and living with the wrong one is miserable in a way that is hard to articulate until you are in the room.

Warm for resting. Neutral for working. Cool for concentrating.

That decision gets made once, for a whole floor. Make it before the batch is ordered, not after.

Buying lighting for a project rather than a room?

Wholesale pricing, white-label options and spec support before you commit to quantities. We would rather spend an hour getting the schedule right than sell you a pallet of the wrong wattage.

DK Lighting has supplied contractors across Pakistan since 2020.
